title: RAG Pipeline Explorer — A Toy Model of Retrieval
description: A clearly labelled toy model of retrieval-augmented generation: a fictional lighthouse handbook is chunked with size and overlap sliders, each chunk gets a deterministic hashed bag-of-words embedding plotted on a 2D PCA map, and a question retrieves the top-k chunks by cosine similarity. See the exact prompt that would be sent within a token budget, and whether the known answer arrived whole, split across a boundary, dropped for budget or missed entirely.
prompt: Build a 'RAG Pipeline Explorer' — a simplified, honest model of retrieval-augmented generation with no real model and no network. Write an original fictional document, chunk it with chunk-size and overlap sliders, give each chunk a deterministic toy embedding (hashed bag-of-words is fine) and plot the chunks on a 2D scatter map. A query should retrieve top-k chunks by cosine similarity with the scores shown, and the page should show exactly what context would be sent to the model and what got missed. Include example questions with known answers so it can say whether the answer made it into the context, and at least one synonym question the toy embedding fails on. Explain the trade-offs (small vs big chunks, overlap, k vs context budget, words vs meaning). Label it clearly as a toy. Night-sky palette — chunks as stars on a map.

methodology: Arithmetic oracle for chunking: the spec computes ceil((N − size) / (size − overlap)) + 1 from the displayed word count and checks the chunk count, stride, duplicated-word count and the number of dots on the map.
Ranking invariants rather than magic numbers: returned scores must be sorted descending and all above the similarity floor, so the test survives tweaks to the toy embedding.

Answer keys as ground truth: each example question has an exact answer span in the document, and the verdict (found / split / dropped for budget / missed) is checked for configurations built to trigger each case.
Negative control: the 'pets' question must miss the 'dogs' passage because a lexical embedding cannot bridge synonyms, while the 'dogs' question must find it.
Budget accounting: after lowering the budget the reported token estimate must stay within it and the overflowing chunks must be marked as dropped.
Responsive check with wider fonts at 360–412px, since the page is dense with long monospace text and sliders.
risks: Signed feature hashing collides: at 64 dimensions the 'dogs' question scored negative against the chunk containing 'Dogs'; moving to 256 dimensions fixed it, and a similarity floor stops zero-score ties from being 'retrieved' by luck.
Changing chunking changes TF-IDF weights and therefore every score, so hard-coded score values in tests would be brittle.
PCA via power iteration can flip axis signs between configurations, so the map's layout is intentionally never asserted.
qa.playwright: Everything is deterministic — no seeds or clocks needed — so the difficulty was choosing oracles that don't just restate the implementation. The spec derives expected chunk counts from a formula, checks ranking order rather than exact scores, and uses answer spans to assert outcomes like 'split across chunks'. The first probe runs were genuinely useful: they exposed hash-collision false negatives and lucky zero-score ties, which changed the design (256 dimensions and a similarity floor). Range sliders are driven with locator.fill(), and the SVG map is checked via data attributes on each point instead of pixels.
coverage: Chunk count, stride, duplicated words and map points for several size/overlap settings; overlap capped below size
Top-k ranking order, similarity floor, context contents and custom questions
Boundary split fixed by overlap; answer longer than a chunk
Context budget drops chunks and can drop the answer

a11y: All knobs are labelled native sliders with live numeric outputs, example questions are buttons, and the retrieval summary and verdict are announced through live regions. Each map point is a focusable, named button that reveals its chunk text, and the ranked list and assembled prompt present the same information as text.
